Anything that reminds me of the person who harmed me
Allowing myself to feel any strong emotion

When I remember the event I feel intense rage

issues.explanation: The trigger 'Arab villages' is hard to reconcile with the trauma type of physical abuse by a romantic partner and the rest of the profile, which centers on interpersonal abuse-related cues, self-appraisals, and memory phenomena. Without any corresponding threat, memory, or appraisal content involving war, military, or ethnic/geographic conflict, this item appears clinically incoherent for this patient.

issues.item: Restrict Eating: control eating strictly to feel in control
issues.explanation: Strictly restricting eating to feel in control is not well supported by the rest of the profile. The other selected items coherently describe PTSD related to partner physical abuse (criticism, violence, offender cues; fragmented/alien memory; rage; dehumanization, self-blame, emotional numbing; distraction and cue avoidance). In contrast, restrictive eating introduces a distinct control-focused coping pattern that is not reflected elsewhere in triggers, memory, threat, or appraisals, making it clinically hard to explain as part of the same formulation rather than a separate problem.

vignette:
At 74, Raymond had the polished, measured manner of a man who had spent a lifetime editing other people's words and suppressing his own. He was divorced, living alone in a small apartment above a print shop, and still working part-time on manuscripts, though lately the work had become harder to trust. The abuse had taken place years earlier, during a relationship with a partner who could turn a dinner table into a battlefield. Raymond remembered one evening in particular: the sharp tone of correction over a trivial remark, the shove that sent him against the kitchen counter, the way the other man's face seemed to harden into something almost unfamiliar. What lingered was not a continuous story but a series of snapshots, each one fixed and vivid in his mind-a hand on his collar, the edge of the sink, the offender standing over him. He said the memory did not feel like his own life at all, as if he were looking at a scene that belonged to someone else, and when it came back he felt a fierce, hot rage that startled him with its intensity.

Those moments had made criticism dangerous in a way that other people did not seem to understand. If a colleague marked up a sentence or a friend corrected a detail, Raymond could feel his body tighten before he had even finished reading the comment. Violence in a film, a raised voice in the street, even the sight of a man who resembled his former partner in build or posture could pull him back into that kitchen with unsettling force. In those moments he found himself reaching almost automatically for distraction-checking email, turning on the radio, scrolling through articles, anything to keep his mind from settling on what he had seen or heard. He also avoided anything that reminded him of the man who harmed him: certain neighborhoods, familiar restaurants, particular aftershaves, even the route he once used to drive to their shared apartment. At work, if an editor-in-chief corrected him in front of others, he would spend the rest of the day buried in copy, deliberately keeping his attention on commas and line breaks so he would not have to feel the surge of anger or fear that rose up under the surface. He had come to believe that allowing himself to feel strong emotion was dangerous, that once he opened the door he might never get control back.

The more Raymond pushed the memory away, the more it seemed to return in fragments. He could be reading a manuscript and suddenly see again the offender's hand, the counter, the look on the man's face; at other times the anger would flash so quickly that he would slam a file shut or leave his desk to walk the block until it passed. Because the recollection arrived as isolated pictures, it never settled into a coherent past event he could place behind him, and because it felt alien, it left him with the strange sense that something had been done to him that had not quite happened to a real person. That was when the old appraisal returned with force: that he was somehow the kind of man this happened to, too passive, too easily managed, not fully a person at all but something to be used. He would tell himself that normal emotions were gone for good, that whatever warmth or ease he once had had been stripped out of him. On bad days he noticed that this belief itself made the memory feel more distant and unreal, as if he were watching yet another scene from outside himself rather than remembering his own life. The sharper his self-blame became, the more the snapshots seemed to detach from him, and the more his mind treated them as evidence that he was already changed in a fundamental way.

Over months, the habit of distraction and avoidance narrowed his world. He stayed late at the office to avoid evening solitude, declined invitations if he thought a guest might be blunt or critical, and kept his apartment quiet so he would not have to notice his own reactions. Yet the very effort to stay away from reminders made him scan for them constantly. A man laughing too loudly in the hallway, an offhand correction from a younger colleague, a television argument from the apartment next door could set him on edge before he had time to explain it to himself. When he then tried to shut down the feeling, the old images came back with greater force, and with them the rage and the sense of being objectified all over again. That in turn made him more certain that something was fundamentally wrong with him, that he was made for this kind of treatment and would never recover the ability to feel normally. By the time he sought help, he was exhausted by the loop itself: frightened by criticism, violence, and any glimpse of the offender; flooded by brief, alien pictures of the assault; and left in a life increasingly organized around keeping emotion out. What finally brought Raymond in was the fear that his shrinking world would become permanent, and the faint hope that he might one day remember what happened to him without feeling less than human.
